questions.q: What is the key difference between an lvalue and an rvalue?
options: Lvalues are always integers; rvalues are always floating point
An lvalue has persistent identity and still exists after the expression; an rvalue is a temporary about to be destroyed
There is no real difference in modern C++
Rvalues can be assigned to, lvalues cannot
questions.explain: An lvalue refers to an object with a lasting identity (you can take its address and it persists). An rvalue is a temporary, such as a function's return value, that's about to be destroyed — which is why the compiler is free to move from it.

questions.q: What does `PriceSeries&& other` in a move constructor's parameter list mean?
options: other is passed by value, as a copy
other is an rvalue reference — it can only bind to a temporary, signaling its resources can be taken
other is a pointer to a PriceSeries
&& means 'and' in a condition
questions.explain: T&& is an rvalue reference, a reference type that binds only to rvalues (temporaries). It signals to the function that it's safe to take ('steal') the referred-to object's internal resources instead of copying them.

questions.q: What does std::move(a) actually do at runtime?
options: It immediately deletes the object a
It physically relocates a's memory to a new address
Nothing at runtime — it's purely a cast that makes a eligible to be treated as an rvalue, so move operations can run instead of copy operations
It copies a and returns the copy
questions.explain: std::move performs no runtime action by itself; it's a cast (static_cast to an rvalue reference) that tells the compiler to consider a as movable, enabling the move constructor or move assignment operator to be selected.

questions.q: After `std::vector<double> b = std::move(a);`, what is the correct way to treat `a`?
options: Continue reading a's elements normally; nothing has changed
a is guaranteed to still contain all its original elements
a is in a valid but unspecified state — safe to destroy or reassign, but its contents should not be read
a is now a dangling pointer and must never be touched again
questions.explain: After being moved from, an object like a std::vector is left in a valid but unspecified state (typically empty for vector). It's safe to destroy or assign a new value to, but you should not rely on its old contents.

questions.q: Why is it considered efficient in modern C++ to return a large object like a std::vector by value from a function?
options: Because the compiler always makes a full copy, which is fast enough not to matter
Because move semantics (and copy elision) let the compiler transfer ownership of the object's resources instead of copying every element
Because std::vector is always allocated on the stack
Because returning by value was always efficient, even before C++11
questions.explain: Since C++11, returning a local object by value is efficient because the compiler can move its resources (or elide the copy/move entirely) rather than deep-copying every element, unlike in pre-C++11 code.
